prompt: Someone spends their day writing and reviewing the code that runs a company's website. Which role is that?
optionA: Data analyst
optionB: Software developer
optionC: Project manager
optionD: Systems administrator
correctAnswerText: Software developer
explanation: Writing and reviewing code is the developer's daily work. An analyst works with data, a manager coordinates the work, and an administrator keeps the systems running.

prompt: Someone spends their day writing queries against a database and preparing reports on what the numbers show. Which role is that?
optionA: Software developer
optionB: Database administrator
optionC: Support engineer
optionD: Data analyst
correctAnswerText: Data analyst
explanation: Querying data and reporting on it is analysis. A database administrator keeps the database itself running, which is adjacent work with different accountability.

prompt: Someone spends their day investigating problems reported by customers and telling the engineering team what is reproducible. Which role is that?
optionA: Support engineer
optionB: Software developer
optionC: Project manager
optionD: Data analyst
correctAnswerText: Support engineer
explanation: Reproducing reported problems and passing them on is support work. A developer may fix what is found, which is the next step rather than the same job.

prompt: Someone spends their day setting up the machines an application runs on and keeping them available. Which role is that?
optionA: Software developer
optionB: Data analyst
optionC: Systems administrator
optionD: Support engineer
correctAnswerText: Systems administrator
explanation: Preparing and maintaining the machines is administration. Writing what runs on them is a different job, though in a small team one person may do both.

prompt: In a very small company, one person writes the code, sets up the servers and answers customer problems. What does that show about roles?
optionA: That the roles are not really distinct
optionB: The work is the same in any company; who does it depends on how many people there are
optionC: That small companies do not need specialists
optionD: That the person holds three jobs at once
correctAnswerText: The work is the same in any company; who does it depends on how many people there are
explanation: The tasks do not merge when one person does them all, which is why a larger team can split them along the same lines. What varies is the division of labour rather than the work.

prompt: What job does a CV do?
optionA: Proves what someone has done
optionB: Lists every task someone has ever performed
optionC: Replaces the need for an interview
optionD: States what someone claims to have done, so a reader can decide whether to look further
correctAnswerText: States what someone claims to have done, so a reader can decide whether to look further
explanation: A CV is a set of claims, which is why it opens a conversation rather than settling one. Anything that could be checked independently is evidence, and a CV is where it is pointed at.

prompt: What job does a portfolio of projects do?
optionA: Shows work a reader can examine for themselves
optionB: Lists the technologies someone has used
optionC: Proves someone worked hard
optionD: Replaces a CV entirely
correctAnswerText: Shows work a reader can examine for themselves
explanation: A portfolio is checkable in a way a claim is not, which is the whole reason for having one. A list of technologies is another claim, in a different format.

prompt: What job does a reference do?
optionA: Adds a formality to the application
optionB: Proves the candidate is a good person
optionC: Lets somebody who worked with the candidate confirm what they did
optionD: Replaces the need for evidence of work
correctAnswerText: Lets somebody who worked with the candidate confirm what they did
explanation: A reference converts a claim into something another person will stand behind. Treating it as a formality is what makes candidates choose referees who cannot say anything specific.

prompt: A candidate needs to show they can build a working application. Which artefact serves that best?
optionA: A CV line saying they can build applications
optionB: A project the reader can run or read
optionC: A certificate from a course about building applications
optionD: A reference saying they are hard-working
correctAnswerText: A project the reader can run or read
explanation: Only one of these lets the reader check the claim rather than accept it. A certificate shows a course was completed, which is a different fact.

prompt: What does an internship expect a candidate to show?
optionA: Several years of experience in the role
optionB: Nothing at all
optionC: A completed degree in the subject
optionD: Enough foundation to learn quickly, rather than experience of the work
correctAnswerText: Enough foundation to learn quickly, rather than experience of the work
explanation: An internship exists to provide the experience, so demanding it would defeat the purpose. That does not make it open to anyone regardless of preparation.

prompt: What does a graduate role expect a candidate to show?
optionA: Foundations and evidence of learning, with training expected on the job
optionB: Nothing, since training is provided
optionC: The same experience as an established developer
optionD: Only a qualification, with nothing further
correctAnswerText: Foundations and evidence of learning, with training expected on the job
explanation: Training being provided sets the level rather than removing the requirement. A qualification is part of what is looked at and rarely the whole of it.

prompt: Is a qualification on its own usually enough to obtain a first role?
optionA: Yes; a qualification is what employers ask for
optionB: No; qualifications are not considered at all
optionC: Rarely; it is one signal among several and says little about what someone can build
optionD: Yes, provided the grade is high enough
correctAnswerText: Rarely; it is one signal among several and says little about what someone can build
explanation: A qualification establishes that a course was completed and leaves open what the candidate can do unsupervised. It is genuinely considered, which is why the answer is "rarely enough" rather than "irrelevant".

prompt: Two routes into a first role are an internship and a graduate programme. What most distinguishes what they expect?
optionA: The internship expects more experience
optionB: The internship expects less prior evidence and offers less certainty of a continuing role
optionC: The graduate programme expects no preparation
optionD: They expect exactly the same things
correctAnswerText: The internship expects less prior evidence and offers less certainty of a continuing role
explanation: The two differ in what they ask for and in what they promise, and both differences run in the same direction. Neither expects nothing.

prompt: Which skill does a data analyst's work depend on most?
optionA: Knowing one particular spreadsheet product
optionB: Communicating clearly, which every role needs
optionC: Designing user interfaces
optionD: Reasoning about what data does and does not support
correctAnswerText: Reasoning about what data does and does not support
explanation: The underlying skill is judgement about evidence; the tools change and the judgement does not. Communication matters everywhere and so does not distinguish this role from any other.

prompt: A job advertisement lists a particular framework. What is the underlying skill it is standing in for?
optionA: Building applications of that kind, which the framework is one way of doing
optionB: Familiarity with that framework and nothing else
optionC: Willingness to learn new tools
optionD: Experience of working in a team
correctAnswerText: Building applications of that kind, which the framework is one way of doing
explanation: A named tool is usually shorthand for the work it is used for, which is why someone with the skill in a different tool is often considered. Reading it as the requirement itself narrows the field to people who happen to have used one product.

prompt: Which of these statements about a candidate can somebody else check?
optionA: That they are passionate about technology
optionB: That they worked very hard on their studies
optionC: A public repository containing an application they wrote
optionD: That they are a fast learner
correctAnswerText: A public repository containing an application they wrote
explanation: Only one of these points at something a reader can open and examine. The others are self-assessments, which may be entirely true and cannot be confirmed by anyone else.

prompt: A candidate lists "completed an online course in databases". Is that evidence of the skill?
optionA: Yes; the course covered the skill
optionB: It is evidence the course was completed, and shows nothing that was built with it
optionC: No; courses are worthless
optionD: Yes, provided the course was long enough
correctAnswerText: It is evidence the course was completed, and shows nothing that was built with it
explanation: Completion is a real and checkable fact about a course rather than about what the candidate can do. A project built afterwards is what turns it into evidence of the skill.

prompt: A candidate built an application that stores records and lets a user search them. Which claimed skill does it support?
optionA: Designing large systems
optionB: Managing a team
optionC: Optimising performance at scale
optionD: Working with stored data and retrieving it
correctAnswerText: Working with stored data and retrieving it
explanation: The project demonstrates what it actually required. The other three are real skills the project gives no evidence about either way.

prompt: A candidate's project uses a payment service through three lines of setup. Does it support a claim of experience with payment systems?
optionA: Weakly; it shows the service was connected rather than that payments were reasoned about
optionB: Yes; the project handles payments
optionC: No; using a service demonstrates nothing at all
optionD: Yes, provided the payments worked
correctAnswerText: Weakly; it shows the service was connected rather than that payments were reasoned about
explanation: Using something trivially is a real but small piece of evidence, and it does not support a claim of depth. Dismissing it entirely overshoots — connecting a service is a genuine, if modest, thing to have done.

prompt: A candidate presents a project as evidence of building a web application. The project was generated from a template and the candidate changed the text and colours. The project does work and is genuinely theirs to show. What does it demonstrate?
optionA: That they can build a web application
optionB: Nothing at all
optionC: That they can run and modify a generated project, not that they can build one
optionD: That they can design interfaces
correctAnswerText: That they can run and modify a generated project, not that they can build one
explanation: What a project demonstrates is what it required of the person presenting it, and here the structure was supplied. It is not worthless — running and modifying a project is something — and it does not support the claim being made.

prompt: A CV says: "Built a booking application (link). Comfortable with databases (link to the same project, which stores bookings). Experienced in team leadership." Which claim is unsupported?
optionA: Built a booking application
optionB: Experienced in team leadership
optionC: Comfortable with databases
optionD: None; all three are supported
correctAnswerText: Experienced in team leadership
explanation: The first two point at a project the reader can open, and the third points at nothing in the document. Being unsupported does not make it untrue, only unverifiable from what is here.

prompt: A CV says: "Reduced page load time from 4 seconds to 1 second on the college portal. Familiar with performance tuning. Passionate about clean code." Which claim is unsupported?
optionA: Reduced page load time from 4 seconds to 1 second
optionB: Familiar with performance tuning
optionC: None; all three are supported
optionD: Passionate about clean code
correctAnswerText: Passionate about clean code
explanation: The stated outcome supports the first and, by implication, the second. The third is a statement about the candidate's feelings and nothing in the document bears on it.

prompt: A CV says: "Led a team of four on a final-year project. Delivered it two weeks early. Expert in distributed systems." The first two claims support each other and the project is described in detail. Which claim is unsupported, and what would support it?
optionA: Expert in distributed systems; something built or operated at that scale would support it
optionB: Led a team of four; a reference would support it
optionC: Delivered two weeks early; a schedule would support it
optionD: None; a detailed project description supports all three
correctAnswerText: Expert in distributed systems; something built or operated at that scale would support it
explanation: The first two are corroborated by the project described, and the third names a capability the project does not touch. Detail elsewhere in a document does not transfer to a claim it says nothing about.

prompt: What most separates a support engineer from a software developer?
optionA: The support engineer is more junior
optionB: The developer uses more tools
optionC: What each is accountable for: reproducing and resolving reported problems against building and changing the product
optionD: The support engineer works fixed hours
correctAnswerText: What each is accountable for: reproducing and resolving reported problems against building and changing the product
explanation: Roles are separated by accountability rather than by seniority, tooling or hours. Any of those may differ at one employer and none of them defines the role.

prompt: What most separates a data analyst from a data engineer?
optionA: The engineer is more senior
optionB: The analyst is accountable for what the data means; the engineer for the pipelines that deliver it
optionC: The analyst uses spreadsheets and the engineer uses code
optionD: They are the same role with different titles
correctAnswerText: The analyst is accountable for what the data means; the engineer for the pipelines that deliver it
explanation: Each owns a different question, which is why both exist on the same team. Tools overlap heavily and vary by employer, so they cannot be the discriminator.

prompt: Two companies advertise a "software engineer" and the described work differs substantially. Both descriptions are accurate for their own company. What follows?
optionA: One of the two companies is using the title wrongly
optionB: The two roles are actually the same and described differently
optionC: Titles are meaningless and should be ignored entirely
optionD: A title is not a reliable guide to the work; the description is what has to be read
correctAnswerText: A title is not a reliable guide to the work; the description is what has to be read
explanation: Titles are not standardised across employers, so the same one covers a range of work. That does not make them meaningless — they narrow the field, and the description settles it.

prompt: A student's stated goal is to become a data analyst. They are offered an unpaid internship writing reports from a company's sales data. Does it advance the goal?
optionA: Yes; it is the work the goal names, and it produces evidence of doing it
optionB: No; it is unpaid
optionC: No; internships do not count as experience
optionD: Yes; any experience advances any goal
correctAnswerText: Yes; it is the work the goal names, and it produces evidence of doing it
explanation: Fit is judged against the stated goal, and this is that work. Being unpaid is a real cost and a separate question from whether it advances the goal.

prompt: A student's stated goal is to become a mobile developer. They are offered a well-paid role testing desktop software. Does it advance the goal?
optionA: Yes; it is a role in technology
optionB: Yes; the pay makes it worthwhile
optionC: Not directly; it builds general experience and not the evidence the goal calls for
optionD: No; it would set the goal back
correctAnswerText: Not directly; it builds general experience and not the evidence the goal calls for
explanation: The opportunity is attractive on other grounds, which is exactly what makes it worth judging against the goal. Not advancing a goal is different from damaging it.

prompt: A student's stated goal is to work on backend systems, and they have stated they cannot relocate. An excellent backend role is offered in another city with no remote option. Does it fit?
optionA: Yes; it is exactly the work the goal names
optionB: It advances the goal and fails a stated constraint, so it is not available on the terms given
optionC: No; it does not advance the goal
optionD: Yes; constraints should give way to a good opportunity
correctAnswerText: It advances the goal and fails a stated constraint, so it is not available on the terms given
explanation: Two things are being asked at once and they come apart here: the fit is perfect and the constraint rules it out. Treating the constraint as negotiable answers a question the student did not ask.

prompt: A student intends to (a) build a project, (b) put it in a public repository, (c) link it from their CV. Which depends on another being done first?
optionA: a depends on c
optionB: b depends on c
optionC: None of them depends on another
optionD: c depends on b, which depends on a
correctAnswerText: c depends on b, which depends on a
explanation: There is nothing to publish until something is built and nothing to link until it is published. The chain runs one way only.

prompt: A student intends to (a) learn a database, (b) learn a testing tool, (c) apply for a role requiring both. Which dependency is real?
optionA: c depends on both a and b; a and b do not depend on each other
optionB: b depends on a
optionC: a depends on b
optionD: All three are independent
correctAnswerText: c depends on both a and b; a and b do not depend on each other
explanation: Applying for something that asks for both requires both, and neither is a prerequisite for the other. Inventing an order between independent steps delays one of them for no reason.

prompt: A student says they must finish their degree before starting any project, because employers want graduates. Employers do prefer graduates for the roles they are aiming at. Is that a real dependency?
optionA: Yes; employers require the degree
optionB: Yes; projects only count after graduation
optionC: No; the preference is real and nothing about building a project requires the degree to be finished first
optionD: No; employers do not prefer graduates
correctAnswerText: No; the preference is real and nothing about building a project requires the degree to be finished first
explanation: The premise is true and the dependency drawn from it is not: a project can be built at any time, and having one at graduation is better than starting then. A preference has been turned into a prerequisite.

prompt: A role requires building web applications, working with databases and using version control. A candidate has a published web application using a database, and no version control history. What is the gap?
optionA: Web applications, which need more depth
optionB: Version control, which the role requires and nothing in the evidence shows
optionC: Databases, which need a larger example
optionD: There is no gap
correctAnswerText: Version control, which the role requires and nothing in the evidence shows
explanation: Two requirements are met by the published project and one is untouched by it. The gap is derived by comparing what is required with what is shown rather than judged impressionistically.

prompt: A role requires database work, testing and public speaking. A candidate has a database project with tests, and no evidence of speaking. Public speaking is listed as desirable rather than required. What is the largest gap against the requirements?
optionA: Public speaking, which is the missing item
optionB: Testing, which needs a larger example
optionC: Database work, which needs to be at a professional scale
optionD: There is none against the requirements; the only gap is in something the role lists as desirable
correctAnswerText: There is none against the requirements; the only gap is in something the role lists as desirable
explanation: The comparison has to be against what is required, and both requirements are evidenced. Reporting the desirable item as the largest gap treats every line of an advertisement as equally binding.

prompt: Two pieces of evidence for database skill: a certificate from a database course, and a working application whose data model the candidate designed. Which establishes more?
optionA: The application, because a reader can examine what was actually designed
optionB: The certificate, because it is formally awarded
optionC: They establish the same amount
optionD: The certificate, because it covers more topics
correctAnswerText: The application, because a reader can examine what was actually designed
explanation: Both are genuine evidence and they show different things: one that a course was passed, the other what the candidate can produce unsupervised. Formality is not the same as informativeness.

prompt: Two pieces of evidence for teamwork: a reference from a manager describing a specific conflict the candidate resolved, and a certificate from a large, well-known teamwork course. The course is more prestigious than the manager's company. Which establishes more?
optionA: The certificate, because the course is better known
optionB: They establish the same amount
optionC: The reference, because it describes something specific that somebody will stand behind
optionD: The certificate, because a reference may be biased
correctAnswerText: The reference, because it describes something specific that somebody will stand behind
explanation: Prestige attaches to the course and says nothing about this candidate, while the reference is about them specifically and is checkable. Bias in a reference is a real concern and does not make a generic certificate more informative.

prompt: Common advice says "build a portfolio of many small projects". A student has one large, genuinely complex application they built over a year. Why might the advice not apply?
optionA: Because portfolios are not useful
optionB: They already have what a portfolio is for — examinable evidence — and depth may serve better than quantity
optionC: Because large projects are always better
optionD: Because the advice is only for beginners
correctAnswerText: They already have what a portfolio is for — examinable evidence — and depth may serve better than quantity
explanation: The advice exists to produce examinable evidence, and this student has it. Its purpose being already met is why it does not apply here, rather than the advice being wrong in general.

prompt: Common advice says "tailor your CV to each application". A student is applying to forty roles with a deadline in three days. The advice is sound and widely followed. Why does it not apply unchanged here?
optionA: Because tailoring a CV does not help
optionB: Because forty applications is too many to make
optionC: Because the advice applies only to senior roles
optionD: The time available makes it impossible for all forty; it applies to the applications they most want
correctAnswerText: The time available makes it impossible for all forty; it applies to the applications they most want
explanation: The advice is good and its cost is what conflicts with the situation, so the answer is to apply it selectively rather than to reject it. Declaring the advice wrong, or the plan wrong, both overshoot.

prompt: Common advice says "apply only to roles you are fully qualified for". Why does that fail for a first role?
optionA: Advertisements routinely list more than a first-role candidate could have, so full qualification would rule out nearly everything
optionB: Because qualifications do not matter
optionC: Because employers do not read applications
optionD: Because the advice is only for experienced candidates
correctAnswerText: Advertisements routinely list more than a first-role candidate could have, so full qualification would rule out nearly everything
explanation: The advice assumes the listed requirements describe a minimum, and for entry-level roles they usually describe an ideal. Following it literally leaves a candidate applying for almost nothing.

prompt: Common advice says "learn the technology that is most in demand". What is the risk in following it without qualification?
optionA: There is no risk; demand is what matters
optionB: Popular technologies are always harder to learn
optionC: Demand shifts, and the underlying skills that transfer are what remain valuable
optionD: The advice is wrong; demand should be ignored
correctAnswerText: Demand shifts, and the underlying skills that transfer are what remain valuable
explanation: Demand is a real signal and a moving one, and what survives a shift is the understanding beneath a particular tool. Ignoring demand entirely is the opposite error and no better.

prompt: A piece of career advice worked well for the person giving it. What does that establish?
optionA: That it will work for anyone
optionB: That it worked in their circumstances; whether it transfers depends on how similar yours are
optionC: That it will not work for anyone else
optionD: Nothing at all; personal experience is worthless
correctAnswerText: That it worked in their circumstances; whether it transfers depends on how similar yours are
explanation: A single success is genuine evidence about one case and says nothing on its own about a different one. Dismissing it entirely discards information that is often the most specific available.

prompt: A student must earn an income from next month and wants to work in software. They are offered a paid support role starting immediately and an unpaid development internship starting in three months. The income constraint is absolute. Which fits, and what does it cost?
optionA: The internship, since it is closer to the goal
optionB: Neither, since neither is ideal
optionC: The support role, at no cost at all
optionD: The support role; it costs the more direct route into development, which can be pursued from inside it
correctAnswerText: The support role; it costs the more direct route into development, which can be pursued from inside it
explanation: A stated absolute constraint decides between the two, and the answer has to name what is given up rather than pretend the choice is free. The internship is better on the goal and unavailable on the terms given.

prompt: A student can accept one of two offers: one matches their goal and requires relocating, which they have said is impossible; the other is remote and unrelated to their goal. What is the honest answer?
optionA: Neither satisfies both; the choice is which to give up, and that decision belongs to the student
optionB: The matching role, since goals matter most
optionC: The remote role, since constraints matter most
optionD: Both are acceptable, so either will do
correctAnswerText: Neither satisfies both; the choice is which to give up, and that decision belongs to the student
explanation: When no option satisfies every constraint, the useful contribution is naming the trade rather than picking a side. Presenting either as simply correct hides the decision being made.

prompt: A student states that salary is their only constraint and then rejects the highest-paid offer. What does that suggest?
optionA: They made a mistake
optionB: The offer must have been withdrawn
optionC: The stated constraint was not the only one; something unstated is also deciding
optionD: Salary constraints are never real
correctAnswerText: The stated constraint was not the only one; something unstated is also deciding
explanation: A decision inconsistent with the stated constraints is evidence that the constraints were incompletely stated. Treating it as an error assumes the statement was complete, which the behaviour contradicts.

prompt: Two roles are offered: one pays more now, the other offers work closer to a stated long-term goal. No constraint rules either out. How should the choice be made?
optionA: Always the higher-paying role
optionB: By deciding how much the sooner income is worth against the goal, which is a judgement the student has to make explicitly
optionC: Always the role closer to the goal
optionD: By whichever offer arrived first
correctAnswerText: By deciding how much the sooner income is worth against the goal, which is a judgement the student has to make explicitly
explanation: With no constraint deciding it, the choice is a genuine trade between two things the student values. A general rule in either direction substitutes somebody else's weighting for theirs.

prompt: A student lists five constraints and no available role satisfies all of them. What is the next step?
optionA: Abandon the search
optionB: Apply anyway and hope one relaxes
optionC: Remove the constraint that is hardest to satisfy
optionD: Establish which constraints are absolute and which are preferences, since only that changes what is available
correctAnswerText: Establish which constraints are absolute and which are preferences, since only that changes what is available
explanation: Constraints that cannot all be met have to be ranked before anything else can happen, and only the student can rank them. Dropping the hardest one is a decision made by difficulty rather than by importance.

prompt: A student aiming to be a front-end developer has spent six months on it and finds the work consistently uninteresting, while enjoying the data work in the same projects. The dislike is consistent across several different projects. Does the evidence support revising the goal?
optionA: Yes; a consistent preference across several projects is evidence about the work rather than about one project
optionB: No; six months is too short to judge
optionC: No; changing goals shows a lack of commitment
optionD: Yes; any dislike justifies changing direction
correctAnswerText: Yes; a consistent preference across several projects is evidence about the work rather than about one project
explanation: What makes this evidence rather than a mood is that it held across several different projects and pointed consistently elsewhere. A single bad experience would not carry the same weight.

prompt: A student aiming to be a developer had one difficult project with an unhelpful team and now wants to abandon the goal. Does the evidence support revising it?
optionA: Yes; a bad experience is evidence
optionB: Yes; enjoyment is what matters most
optionC: Not on its own; the difficulty was about that team rather than about the work
optionD: No; goals should never be revised
correctAnswerText: Not on its own; the difficulty was about that team rather than about the work
explanation: The evidence is about the circumstances rather than the work, so it does not speak to the goal. That is different from saying a goal should never change.

prompt: A student discovers that the role they were aiming for involves far less of the work they enjoy than they had assumed. What does that support?
optionA: Persisting, since the goal was chosen deliberately
optionB: Revising the goal, since it was formed on a picture of the work that turns out to be wrong
optionC: Persisting, since assumptions can be adjusted later
optionD: Nothing; assumptions about roles are always wrong
correctAnswerText: Revising the goal, since it was formed on a picture of the work that turns out to be wrong
explanation: A goal chosen on a mistaken picture rests on something the evidence has now removed. Revising it is what the new information supports, rather than a failure of resolve.

prompt: Revising a goal costs the progress already made towards it; persisting costs time if the goal is wrong. How should the two be weighed?
optionA: By the progress already made, which should not be wasted
optionB: By whichever costs less time overall
optionC: They cannot be weighed; the choice is arbitrary
optionD: By what the evidence says about the goal, since progress already made is spent either way
correctAnswerText: By what the evidence says about the goal, since progress already made is spent either way
explanation: Effort already spent cannot be recovered by continuing, so it is not a reason to continue. What remains is what the evidence now says about whether the goal is the right one.
